Definition
In this lesson, you will troubleshoot faults in a PCM transmitter and receiver system.
INTRODUCTIONM
Troubleshooting PCM systems is not difficult due to the use of digital chips.
Measuring the input and output signals of a chip determines if the chip is faulted. That's all there is to it!
However, due to the vast number of chips used in a PCM system, and the few discrete components used, you need a plan in order to isolate a problem in a circuit.

After the fault has been isolated to the transmitter or receiver, and then isolated to a particular circuit, you can then use all your previously learned digital troubleshooting techniques to identify the failed chip or component.
Let's begin the lesson on PCM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING.....................

PCM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
In this experiment, you will locate the failed chip or component in a PCM transmitter and receiver system.
EXPERIMENT
PC130-326 SCHEMATIC - Transmitter
The transmitter consists of amplifier, A/D converter, P/S converter, Output Multiplexer and Timer/Sync Bit Generator circuits.
PC130-327 SCHEMATIC - Receiver
The receiver consists of amplifiers, S/P converter, D/A converter, Sync Bit Detector and Timing circuits.
To locate a faulted chip, you must first determine if the PCM system is operating correctly.
This is accomplished by making one simple oscilloscope measurement. Measure the input to the transmitter and the output of the receiver.
If the output signal matches the input signal, the PCM system is operating correctly.
If you do not have a good signal on the output of the receiver, the system is faulted.
Once you have determined that the PCM system is not operating correctly, you must then isolate the fault to either the transmitter, transmission medium or receiver.
This is accomplished by making two simple oscilloscope measurements.
First, measure the output of the transmitter.
If a PCM signal is present, the transmitter circuit must be operating correctly.
If the PCM signal is not present, the transmitter is faulted.
Second, measure the input to the receiver. You already know that the receiver has a bad output or you would not be troubleshooting the system.
If an attenuated PCM signal is not present on the input, the fault is in the transmission medium.
If an attenuated PCM signal is present on the output, the fault is in the receiver.
If the fault is in the transmission medium, checking out the antenna or transmission cables will normally locate the failure.
If the fault is in the transmitter, oscilloscope measurements will isolate the fault to circuit.
If the fault is in the receiver, oscilloscope measurements will isolate the fault to a circuit.

A better method is to input an AC signal that will produce a recognizable pattern in the PCM data. In this way, just looking at the PCM signal will indicate that the system is operating correctly.

This is the method that you will use. You will input a low frequency triangle waveform. The PCM data should then appear to count up from 00000000 to 11111111 on the raising portion and count down from 11111111 to 00000000 on the failing portion of the triangle wave.
2. Select the triangle output of the function generator.
3. Select 1 Hz output frequency from the function generator. 4. Set the output amplitude of the function generator to 10 Vpp from 0 V to +10 V as seen on CH1, use the DC offset.
The information output signal of the receiver should be the same as the information input signal to the transmitter.
5. Move the CH1 probe to the PC130-326 OUTPUT TP.
6. Move the CH2 probe to the PC130-327 INPUT TP.

7. Use external triggering for the oscilloscope from the PC 130- 326 SYNC TP. You should be viewing the PCM data. Notice that it is counting up and counting down. This is a quick way to determine if the transmitter is operating correctly without doing calculations.

As a final note before starting the troubleshooting problems: Use CH1 triggering when viewing the input signal to the transmitter and the output signal of the receiver. Use external triggering (PC130-326 SYNC TP) when viewing signals inside the transmitter and receiver.

The computer will now insert a fault, or insert no fault, into the PCM system. You are to determine if the system is operating correctly, and if not, you are to locate the fault to the transmitter or receiver, to the circuit, and then to the most probable chip.
